title: Stroke and TIA: Time Is Brain
bottomLine: A new focal neurologic deficit is stroke until proven otherwise. Establish last-known-well, check glucose, activate emergency stroke care and obtain urgent brain plus vascular imaging; transient symptoms within 48 hours remain high risk and are not 'reassuring' because they resolved.
recognize: Sudden unilateral weakness/numbness, facial droop, aphasia/dysarthria, visual field loss, neglect, ataxia or severe posterior-circulation symptoms can indicate stroke.
TIA causes transient focal neurologic dysfunction without reassuring the clinician about short-term risk.

Canadian Stroke Best Practices classifies new stroke/TIA symptoms within 48 hours—especially motor or speech symptoms—as highest-risk for recurrence and recommends immediate stroke-capable ED assessment.
differentiate: Check glucose because hypoglycemia can mimic stroke.
Seizure with postictal deficit, migraine aura, Bell palsy and functional symptoms can mimic stroke, but do not delay acute stroke evaluation when the presentation is plausible.
Isolated peripheral facial weakness involving the forehead differs from typical cortical facial weakness but atypical features still require careful assessment.
assessment: Document exact onset/last-known-well, anticoagulants, recent surgery/bleeding, baseline function and stroke symptoms.
Perform rapid neurologic assessment while maintaining ABCs; do not allow a long comprehensive exam to delay transfer/imaging.
workup: Urgent noncontrast brain imaging plus neurovascular imaging is central to acute assessment; obtain glucose and acute-care laboratory tests without delaying reperfusion decisions.
Evaluate cardiac rhythm and vascular risk after the immediate emergency phase.
management: Activate EMS/stroke pathway; suspected acute stroke needs a stroke-enabled ED rather than office observation.
Reperfusion eligibility is time- and imaging-dependent; acute stroke specialists determine thrombolysis/thrombectomy candidacy.
TIA/non-disabling stroke requires urgent secondary prevention based on mechanism, including antithrombotic, BP/lipid and AF management when appropriate.
medicationSafety: Do not give antiplatelet therapy before intracranial hemorrhage has been excluded in a new acute stroke presentation.
Anticoagulant use and timing influence reperfusion decisions; provide exact drug/dose/last dose to the acute team.
redFlags: Severe sudden headache with neurologic deficit
counselling: Teach FAST/stroke warning signs and that transient symptoms still require emergency evaluation.
followUp: Ensure mechanism-specific secondary prevention and rapid follow-up after TIA/minor stroke; close the loop on vascular imaging and rhythm monitoring.
examTrap: Scheduling an outpatient neurology visit because the weakness resolved after 20 minutes.
oneLinePearl: Resolved focal deficits can be the warning shot—TIA within 48 hours is an emergency pathway.
sourceBasis: Canadian Stroke Best Practices Acute Stroke Management 7th Edition with 2025 EVT Interim Update
Canadian Stroke Best Practices TIA/Minor Stroke Recommendations

title: Headache: Red Flags Before Migraine
bottomLine: Diagnose primary headache clinically only after looking for secondary red flags. A typical recurrent migraine with a normal neurologic examination usually does not need neuroimaging; thunderclap, new neurologic signs, pregnancy/postpartum concern, systemic disease or a major pattern change does.
recognize: Migraine commonly produces recurrent moderate-severe headache with nausea and/or photophobia/phonophobia, often worsened by activity; aura is usually fully reversible and evolves over minutes.
Medication-overuse headache should be considered when acute treatments are used frequently and headache becomes increasingly frequent.
differentiate: Thunderclap onset raises subarachnoid hemorrhage and vascular causes.

New headache with fever/meningismus, cancer/immunosuppression, papilledema, focal deficit, pregnancy/postpartum hypertension, age-related giant-cell arteritis features or positional/exertional triggers requires secondary workup.
Cluster headache produces severe strictly unilateral orbital/temporal pain with ipsilateral autonomic features and restlessness.
assessment: Ask onset speed, first/worst status, previous pattern, frequency, duration, triggers, aura, neurologic symptoms, pregnancy/postpartum status, systemic symptoms and medication days/month.
Perform neurologic exam and funduscopic assessment when indicated.
workup: Do not routinely image a stable typical migraine with normal neurologic examination.
Choose CT/CTA, MRI/MRA, lumbar puncture or inflammatory testing based on the suspected secondary cause and timing.
management: Treat acute migraine early with an evidence-based strategy matched to severity and contraindications; triptans/gepants or other migraine-specific therapy may be appropriate when simple analgesics are inadequate.

Consider prevention when attack frequency/disability or acute-treatment burden justifies it; the 2024 Canadian Headache Society guideline includes traditional preventives, CGRP-targeting therapies and onabotulinumtoxinA for appropriate patients.
Address sleep, hydration, regular meals, exercise, triggers and medication overuse without implying lifestyle caused the disease.
medicationSafety: Avoid vasoconstrictive triptans in relevant vascular contraindications and review pregnancy-specific options.
Frequent acute medication use can perpetuate medication-overuse headache; preventive therapy may be safer than escalating rescue use.
redFlags: New headache after age 50 with GCA features
counselling: Use a headache diary to track frequency, disability and acute medication use.
Teach which headache changes require emergency evaluation rather than routine migraine treatment.
followUp: Reassess preventive efficacy after an adequate trial and monitor frequency of acute medication use.
examTrap: Ordering CT/MRI for every classic migraine—or calling a thunderclap headache 'migraine' because the patient has a migraine history.
oneLinePearl: A familiar migraine needs treatment; an unfamiliar headache needs explanation.
sourceBasis: Canadian Headache Society Migraine Prevention Guideline 2024
Choosing Wisely Canada Headache Imaging Guidance

title: First Seizure and Seizure Emergencies
bottomLine: For a first seizure, separate provoked from unprovoked events and rule out immediate reversible threats. Ongoing convulsive seizure/status is an emergency; a recovered stable patient still needs cause-directed evaluation, safety counselling and driving guidance.
recognize: Witnessed tonic-clonic activity, lateral tongue injury, postictal confusion and amnesia support seizure but no single feature is definitive.
Provoking causes include hypoglycemia, sodium disturbance, alcohol/sedative withdrawal, infection, toxins, stroke and medication effects.
differentiate: Syncope can include brief myoclonic jerks but usually has rapid recovery once supine and a characteristic trigger/prodrome.
Psychogenic nonepileptic seizures require careful diagnosis and do not justify dismissing future medical events.
A first focal seizure in an older adult raises structural disease until evaluated.
assessment: ABCs, glucose, injury, pregnancy, fever, medication/substance history and exact witness description.
Ask about prior subtle focal events, sleep deprivation, alcohol/benzodiazepine changes and family history.
workup: Use electrolytes/glucose and other cause-directed labs; neuroimaging is urgent when focal deficit, head trauma, immunocompromise, cancer, anticoagulation, fever or persistent altered state raises structural concern.
Arrange EEG and appropriate MRI for unprovoked seizure through the local pathway.
management: Treat ongoing convulsive seizure with emergency benzodiazepine-based protocol and escalate for status epilepticus.
Correct reversible metabolic/toxic causes.
Long-term antiseizure medication after a first unprovoked seizure depends on recurrence risk, imaging/EEG and patient context rather than an automatic prescription.
medicationSafety: Abrupt benzodiazepine/alcohol withdrawal can provoke seizures.
Antiseizure medications have pregnancy/contraception interactions and teratogenic considerations; counsel before conception where possible.
redFlags: Seizure lasting or recurring without recovery
counselling: Discuss bathing/swimming/heights/machinery safety, sleep and substance triggers.
Driving restrictions are provincial/territorial and diagnosis-specific; document counselling and follow local reporting rules.
followUp: Ensure neurology/first-seizure pathway follow-up and review pending EEG/imaging.
examTrap: Starting chronic antiseizure medication for every single provoked seizure without first correcting the cause and estimating recurrence risk.
oneLinePearl: First seizure: stabilize, find the provocation, then estimate recurrence risk.

title: Dizziness and Vertigo: Central or Peripheral?
bottomLine: Do not diagnose dizziness by adjectives alone. Use timing, triggers, targeted examination and neurologic red flags to separate benign peripheral syndromes from posterior-circulation stroke, arrhythmia, orthostasis and metabolic disease.
recognize: BPPV causes brief triggered episodes with position change and characteristic positional nystagmus.
Vestibular neuritis causes acute persistent vertigo without hearing loss; labyrinthitis adds auditory symptoms.
Central causes are more likely with focal neurologic findings, severe truncal/gait ataxia, direction-changing/vertical nystagmus or high vascular risk.
differentiate: Lightheadedness/presyncope needs cardiovascular/orthostatic evaluation rather than a vestibular diagnosis.
HINTS is useful only in the appropriate acute vestibular syndrome and in clinicians trained to perform/interpret it; misuse can falsely reassure.
assessment: Characterize timing and triggers; examine eye movements/nystagmus, gait, cerebellar function, hearing, focal neurology and orthostatic vitals when appropriate.
Review sedatives, antihypertensives, hypoglycemics and alcohol.
workup: Typical BPPV usually needs no imaging.
Urgent stroke imaging is indicated when central features or high-risk acute vestibular syndrome are present; test glucose/ECG for nonvestibular mimics.
management: Treat BPPV with an appropriate canalith repositioning maneuver rather than chronic vestibular suppressants.
Use short-term antiemetic/vestibular suppressants selectively for severe acute peripheral symptoms; prolonged use can impede compensation.
Central suspicion requires emergency stroke pathway.
medicationSafety: Sedating vestibular suppressants increase falls, particularly in older adults.
Avoid assuming dizziness after a medication change is benign without checking BP, rhythm and neurologic status.
redFlags: New unilateral hearing loss with neurologic concern
counselling: Teach safe positional maneuvers when appropriate and fall precautions during active vertigo.
followUp: Persistent or atypical vertigo needs reassessment rather than indefinite meclizine/dimenhydrinate refills.
examTrap: Calling all spinning dizziness BPPV and prescribing a vestibular suppressant without checking gait or neurologic findings.
oneLinePearl: Timing plus triggers plus exam beats the word 'dizzy'.

title: Acute Abdominal Pain: Don't Miss the Surgical Patient
bottomLine: Abdominal pain is a disposition problem before it is a final-diagnosis problem. Look for shock, peritonitis, pregnancy emergencies, obstruction, ischemia, perforation, appendicitis and other time-sensitive causes before treating presumed benign disease.
recognize: Peritonitis, rigid abdomen, involuntary guarding, pain out of proportion, GI bleeding, persistent vomiting, fever with instability or toxic appearance are concerning.
Older adults and immunocompromised patients may have muted tenderness/fever despite serious disease.
Pregnancy testing is a core discriminator in reproductive-age patients when pregnancy is possible.
differentiate: Pain migration and associated symptoms change the differential more than the numeric pain score.
Cardiac, pulmonary, metabolic and genitourinary disease can present as abdominal pain.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, pain onset/location/migration, vomiting/stool/urine, bleeding, fever, prior surgery, medications/NSAIDs/anticoagulants and pregnancy possibility.
Perform focused abdominal and relevant pelvic/testicular/cardiopulmonary exam based on presentation.
workup: Use CBC, electrolytes/renal function, liver/pancreatic tests, urinalysis, pregnancy test, ECG/troponin or imaging only as guided by the differential.
Choose ultrasound preferentially when it answers the question without radiation, including many biliary/pelvic/pregnancy presentations.
management: Give analgesia and antiemetics while evaluating; appropriate pain treatment does not prevent diagnosis.
Escalate suspected peritonitis, ischemia, perforation, obstruction with compromise, ectopic pregnancy or hemodynamic instability.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs may worsen GI bleeding/renal disease; opioids can obscure sedation/respiratory status but should not be withheld when severe pain warrants them with monitoring.
counselling: If outpatient management is appropriate, give specific return precautions for worsening pain, fever, vomiting, bleeding, syncope or inability to hydrate.
followUp: Undifferentiated pain needs a defined reassessment interval rather than 'follow up as needed'.
examTrap: Ordering a broad lab panel and waiting for results before recognizing peritonitis or shock.
oneLinePearl: Before naming the abdomen, decide whether it is surgical or unstable.

title: Upper GI Bleeding
bottomLine: GI bleed management starts with hemodynamics, not endoscopy labels. Stabilize, quantify severity, review antithrombotics/NSAIDs and obtain urgent endoscopic-capable care when significant bleeding is suspected.
recognize: Hematemesis, coffee-ground emesis and melena suggest upper GI bleeding; brisk upper bleeding can cause hematochezia.
Tachycardia, orthostasis, syncope, hypotension and altered mentation indicate clinically important blood loss.
Early hemoglobin can be deceptively normal before plasma equilibration.
differentiate: Variceal and nonvariceal bleeding require different adjunctive treatment; known cirrhosis/portal hypertension changes the acute plan.
Iron/bismuth can darken stool but do not explain hemodynamic instability or a positive bleeding history.
assessment: ABCs, vitals/orthostatics when safe, volume status, stool/emesis description, NSAID use, anticoagulant/antiplatelet use, alcohol/liver disease and prior ulcer/bleed.
Look for chronic liver disease and alternative bleeding sources.
workup: CBC, type and screen/crossmatch as severity warrants, electrolytes/renal function, INR/coagulation where relevant and liver tests.
Use validated risk tools in the appropriate setting to support disposition, not replace clinical instability assessment.
management: Establish IV access and resuscitate clinically significant bleeding; arrange urgent hospital/endoscopy pathway.
Use proton-pump inhibitor and variceal-specific therapy according to the suspected source and acute-care protocol.
Manage anticoagulant reversal selectively based on severity, drug and thrombotic risk rather than automatically reversing every patient.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs increase ulcer/rebleeding risk; review gastroprotection and necessity.
Restarting antithrombotic therapy after bleeding requires balancing rebleeding against thrombotic harm and should have an explicit plan.
counselling: After stabilization, address H. pylori/NSAID risks and medication adherence where relevant.
followUp: Ensure pathology/H. pylori results, medication changes and repeat blood counts/endoscopy follow-up are closed-loop.
examTrap: Using the initial hemoglobin as proof that a patient with hematemesis and shock has not lost much blood.
oneLinePearl: In GI bleeding, physiology tells you severity before hemoglobin does.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology Upper GI Bleeding Guidelines
CAG/ACG Antithrombotic Management During Acute GI Bleeding 2022

title: Dyspepsia and GERD: Alarm Features Matter
bottomLine: Most dyspepsia/GERD is managed clinically, but age, progressive dysphagia, GI bleeding, anemia, weight loss, persistent vomiting or other alarm features change the threshold for endoscopy and alternative diagnosis.
recognize: GERD commonly causes heartburn/regurgitation; dyspepsia includes epigastric pain/burning, early satiety or postprandial fullness.
Chest pain must be assessed for cardiac disease before being labelled reflux when the presentation is concerning.
differentiate: Dysphagia/odynophagia, bleeding, anemia, unintentional weight loss and persistent vomiting are not routine uncomplicated reflux.
H. pylori-related dyspepsia requires a test-and-treat strategy in appropriate patients and confirmation of eradication when indicated.
assessment: Clarify reflux vs dyspepsia symptoms, dysphagia, bleeding, weight loss, NSAIDs, alcohol, smoking, pregnancy and cardiac risk.
Review response and duration of previous acid suppression.
workup: Use H. pylori testing and/or endoscopy according to age, risk and alarm features; stop acid-suppressing agents for the required interval before certain H. pylori tests when applicable.
Do not routinely image uncomplicated reflux.
management: Lifestyle measures should be individualized to actual triggers; weight management may help where relevant without stigmatizing the patient.
Use an appropriate PPI trial for typical GERD/dyspepsia when indicated, then step down to the lowest effective strategy if symptoms allow.
Eradicate H. pylori using current local/national regimens that account for antimicrobial resistance and confirm eradication when recommended.
medicationSafety: Long-term PPIs should have a continuing indication; do not stop abruptly in high-risk bleeding prevention situations solely because of generalized PPI fears.
Review NSAID/antithrombotic ulcer risk.
counselling: Explain appropriate duration and purpose of acid suppression and why alarm symptoms need endoscopic evaluation.
followUp: Reassess persistent symptoms after an adequate treatment strategy; confirm H. pylori eradication when applicable.
examTrap: Increasing the PPI indefinitely in a patient with progressive dysphagia instead of arranging endoscopic evaluation.
oneLinePearl: Reflux is common; alarm features are not.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology Dyspepsia and Upper GI Guidelines

title: RUQ and Epigastric Pain: Biliary Disease or Pancreatitis?
bottomLine: Distinguish uncomplicated biliary colic from cholecystitis, cholangitis and pancreatitis because the disposition changes. Fever plus jaundice plus RUQ pain signals biliary infection/obstruction requiring urgent source control, not outpatient analgesia.
recognize: Biliary colic: episodic postprandial RUQ/epigastric pain without systemic inflammation.
Cholecystitis: persistent RUQ pain/tenderness with inflammatory features.
Cholangitis: biliary obstruction plus infection; fever, jaundice and RUQ pain are classic.
Pancreatitis: persistent severe epigastric pain often radiating to back plus elevated pancreatic enzymes/imaging context.
differentiate: Normal lipase makes acute pancreatitis less likely when timed appropriately; very high liver enzymes/bilirubin can suggest obstruction.
Acalculous cholecystitis occurs in critically ill patients and can be easy to miss.
assessment: Assess vitals, hydration, peritonitis, jaundice, alcohol, gallstone history, triglycerides and causative medications.
Ask about pregnancy and previous biliary procedures.
workup: RUQ ultrasound is first-line for suspected gallbladder disease; liver tests and lipase guide differentiation.
Use advanced imaging/MRCP/ERCP based on obstruction/cholangitis suspicion rather than routinely.
management: Cholangitis requires urgent hospital care, antibiotics and biliary decompression pathway.
Acute cholecystitis needs surgical assessment; pancreatitis is largely supportive with fluids/analgesia/early nutrition as tolerated while treating the cause.
Do not give prophylactic antibiotics for uncomplicated sterile pancreatitis.
medicationSafety: Review GLP-1RA and other medication histories without assuming causality when gallstone/alcohol causes are more likely.
NSAIDs may be unsuitable with kidney injury/GI risk.
counselling: After gallstone pancreatitis/cholecystitis, explain recurrence prevention and definitive gallbladder management pathway.
followUp: Ensure etiologic workup and surgical/GI follow-up after acute stabilization.
examTrap: Calling fever, jaundice and RUQ pain simple biliary colic and sending the patient home with analgesics.
oneLinePearl: RUQ pain + fever + jaundice is an obstruction/infection emergency until proven otherwise.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology Guideline Library

title: Acute Diarrhea: Hydrate, Then Decide Who Needs Testing
bottomLine: Most acute watery diarrhea is self-limited and needs hydration, not antibiotics or stool panels. Test and escalate when there is severe dehydration, blood, high fever/systemic toxicity, immunocompromise, outbreak/travel risk, prolonged illness or suspected C. difficile.
recognize: Watery diarrhea without severe systemic features is usually supportive-care territory.
Bloody diarrhea, severe abdominal pain, high fever or sepsis changes the differential toward invasive pathogens/inflammatory disease/ischemia.
Recent antibiotics or healthcare exposure raises C. difficile risk.
differentiate: Avoid antimotility agents in severe inflammatory/bloody diarrhea or suspected toxic megacolon.
Empiric antibiotics can be harmful in some Shiga-toxin-producing E. coli scenarios; do not reflexively treat bloody diarrhea before considering the pathogen/risk context.
assessment: Assess dehydration, duration/frequency, blood, fever, vomiting, travel, food/water exposures, sick contacts, antibiotics, immunocompromise and public-health/outbreak context.
workup: Reserve stool testing for cases where results will change treatment, infection control or public-health action.
Check electrolytes/renal function when dehydration or severe disease is present.
management: Oral rehydration is first-line when tolerated; IV fluids if severe dehydration or inability to drink.
Use antibiotics only for defined indications and according to organism/local guidance.
Implement infection-control/public-health measures when required.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary antibiotics because they increase adverse effects, resistance and C. difficile risk.
Renally adjust medications during dehydration/AKI risk.
redFlags: Infant/older frail patient unable to hydrate
counselling: Teach oral rehydration, hand hygiene and when to seek reassessment; food exclusion/work restrictions depend on local public-health rules.
followUp: Persistent or recurrent diarrhea needs broader evaluation for inflammatory, malabsorptive, medication and chronic infectious causes.
examTrap: Ordering a multiplex stool panel and empiric antibiotics for every 24-hour episode of watery diarrhea.
oneLinePearl: Most diarrhea needs fluid; the red flags decide who needs a pathogen hunt.

title: Low Back Pain: Red Flags and Cauda Equina
bottomLine: Most mechanical low back pain does not need imaging. Image/escalate for cauda equina, infection, malignancy, fracture or major neurologic deficit—not because pain is severe or has lasted a few days.
recognize: Mechanical pain often varies with movement and lacks systemic or progressive neurologic features.
Radicular pain follows a nerve-root pattern and may include sensory/reflex/motor changes.
Cauda equina concern rises with new urinary retention/overflow, saddle anesthesia, bilateral/progressive weakness or major bowel dysfunction.
differentiate: Urinary frequency from pain/anxiety is not the same as painless retention; objective post-void residual can help when symptoms are unclear.
Cancer, epidural infection and vertebral fracture have distinct risk contexts such as malignancy history, immunosuppression/IV drug use/fever, trauma/osteoporosis/steroids.
assessment: Ask red flags, trauma, cancer, infection risk, steroid use and neurologic symptoms; perform strength, sensation, reflexes, gait and relevant saddle/perianal assessment when cauda equina is plausible.
Assess bladder function rather than asking only 'any urinary symptoms?'.
workup: No routine imaging for uncomplicated nonspecific low back pain.
Urgent MRI/ED/spine pathway for cauda equina or epidural compression suspicion; image fracture/infection/malignancy based on risk.
management: For uncomplicated pain, encourage activity as tolerated, education and nonpharmacologic measures with targeted analgesia.
Avoid unnecessary bed rest and routine opioids.
Emergency surgical evaluation is required for cauda equina/major compressive neurologic syndrome.
medicationSafety: NSAID choice must account for CKD, GI bleeding, anticoagulation, HF and pregnancy.
Muscle relaxants/sedatives can impair function and increase falls.
redFlags: Cancer history with new persistent pain
counselling: Explain that early imaging in uncomplicated pain often does not improve outcomes and can identify incidental abnormalities.
Give explicit return precautions for new weakness, saddle numbness or bladder/bowel dysfunction.
followUp: Reassess persistent pain or new neurologic findings; shift to active rehabilitation for subacute/chronic mechanical pain.
examTrap: Reassuring a patient with new urinary retention and saddle numbness because straight-leg raise is negative.
oneLinePearl: Back pain plus bladder/saddle/progressive weakness = think cauda equina now.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Back Pain Imaging Principles

title: Hot Swollen Joint: Septic Until Safely Excluded
bottomLine: Acute monoarthritis is septic arthritis until the clinical probability is acceptably low. Gout does not protect the patient from infection; crystals and bacteria can coexist.
recognize: Septic arthritis often presents with acute severe pain, restricted passive range of motion, warmth/swelling and sometimes fever; older/immunocompromised patients may lack fever.
Gout commonly affects the first MTP but can involve knees/ankles and may be triggered by diuretics, CKD, alcohol or illness.
differentiate: Serum uric acid can be normal during an acute gout flare and does not diagnose the cause of a hot joint.
Cellulitis, bursitis, trauma and pseudogout can mimic intra-articular infection.
assessment: Assess fever/systemic toxicity, prosthetic joint, immunosuppression, recent procedure, skin infection, STI risk, trauma and prior crystal disease.
Determine whether pain is primarily with passive joint movement versus periarticular structures.
workup: Urgent arthrocentesis for synovial cell count/differential, Gram stain/culture and crystals when septic arthritis is plausible; obtain blood cultures if systemically ill.
Do not delay aspiration solely to obtain serum uric acid or imaging.
management: Septic arthritis requires urgent hospital/orthopedic assessment, drainage and IV antimicrobial therapy after cultures when feasible without dangerous delay.
Treat confirmed/strongly supported gout with anti-inflammatory therapy chosen for comorbidity and timing; do not stop chronic urate-lowering therapy during a flare solely because of the flare.
medicationSafety: NSAIDs/colchicine require renal/GI/drug-interaction assessment.
Systemic steroids can worsen occult infection; do not inject/treat presumed gout with steroids before excluding septic arthritis when probability is significant.
counselling: For gout, address urate-lowering adherence, trigger myths and cardiovascular/renal comorbidity rather than focusing only on dietary purine restriction.
followUp: Septic arthritis requires culture/result follow-up; recurrent gout needs long-term urate strategy after the acute episode.
examTrap: Diagnosing gout because crystals are present and failing to send a synovial culture.
oneLinePearl: Crystals do not sterilize a joint.

title: Osteoporosis and Fracture Prevention
bottomLine: Osteoporosis care is fracture-risk care, not simply a T-score chase. Identify fragility fractures and fall risks, use Canadian FRAX/BMD criteria, treat high-risk patients and never stop denosumab without an antiresorptive transition plan.
recognize: A prior hip/vertebral or multiple fragility fractures can establish high fracture risk even before looking at a T-score.
Osteoporosis Canada 2023 recommends targeted BMD testing based on age plus clinical risk rather than screening every younger adult.
Falls, glucocorticoids, low body weight, smoking, alcohol, parental hip fracture and secondary causes modify risk.
differentiate: Osteoarthritis pain is not osteoporosis; osteoporosis is usually silent until fracture.
A low BMD is one component of fracture risk; age and prior fractures can outweigh a modest T-score difference.
assessment: Ask prior fragility fracture, falls, height loss, glucocorticoids, smoking/alcohol, parent hip fracture, secondary causes and medication adherence.
Assess gait/balance and physical signs suggesting vertebral compression.
workup: Use BMD and Canada-specific FRAX (preferred) or CAROC to estimate 10-year fracture risk in the guideline population.
Investigate calcium, creatinine, alkaline phosphatase, TSH and other secondary causes when indicated; image suspected vertebral fractures.
management: Use progressive resistance/balance/functional exercise and adequate calcium/vitamin D nutrition.
Bisphosphonates are first-line for most people starting pharmacotherapy; the choice is individualized for renal function, GI issues, adherence and fracture risk.
Denosumab requires long-term continuity or a planned bisphosphonate transition because abrupt discontinuation can cause rapid bone loss and vertebral fractures.
medicationSafety: Check renal function and administration requirements for bisphosphonates.
Plan dental/atypical-fracture counselling proportionate to risk without exaggerating rare harms compared with fracture prevention benefit.
Do not create an unplanned denosumab 'drug holiday'.
redFlags: New severe back pain/height loss suggesting vertebral fracture
counselling: Explain absolute fracture risk and benefits/harms of therapy; address fall prevention and home safety.
followUp: Osteoporosis Canada suggests BMD monitoring about 3 years after starting pharmacotherapy in many patients, with earlier individualized review for new fracture or major risk change.
examTrap: Stopping denosumab for a routine 'drug holiday' without transition therapy.
oneLinePearl: Treat fracture risk, not just bone density—and never abandon denosumab without a bridge.
